Acclaim

/uh-KLAYM/ - rhymes with flame · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Acclaim means high praise.

Her debut poetry collection, printed by a tiny press, gathered such acclaim that bookstores could not keep it shelved.

Worked Example

The indie studio's little puzzle game, built by four friends in a garage, earned worldwide acclaim within a month — glowing write-ups, fan letters, and a shelf of imitators by spring.

Acclaim is stronger and more public than praise: praise can come from one person in private, while acclaim is applause-level approval arriving from many directions at once — critics, audiences, whole professions. It is also praise for merit, which separates it from mere fame: plenty of people are famous without ever being acclaimed.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

admiration: Admiration is the respectful, warm feeling an audience has for good work, and it can stay entirely private — you can admire a poet and never say so. Acclaim is that feeling made loud and public: many voices praising at once, out where everyone can hear it.

renown: Renown is the state of being widely known — a name that travels far beyond its own field. Acclaim is the praise itself, not the being known: a scientist can enjoy renown while rivals dispute her every finding, but acclaim exists only where the reviews are warm.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

criticism: pointed fault-finding, the opposite verdict

scorn: contempt that refuses to take the work seriously at all

Where it sits · how many voices join the chorus — approval → praise → acclaim

approval vs. acclaim: Approval is a passing grade — a nod that the work is acceptable; acclaim is far louder and warmer than that.

praise vs. acclaim: Praise stops a step short of acclaim: one reviewer praises; when every reviewer praises at once, the chorus is acclaim.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ac-

Prefix — ac-: to, toward (Latin ad-)

Root — claim

Root — claim: to shout, cry out (Latin clamare)

Put it together

Put it together: Ac- (toward) + claim (to shout, from Latin clamare) = to shout toward someone — and the noun acclaim is that shouting: approval loud enough to sound like a crowd calling your name. English keeps the same root in exclaim (to shout out) and proclaim (to shout forth).

Use the root in a new word: exclaim

Use the root in a new word: exclaim: 'That's the missing key!' she exclaimed, holding the little brass thing over her head.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / journalistic

Reach for acclaim when praise is public and comes from many directions — critics, audiences, a whole field. For one person's kind words, praise is the honest size. Keep its unit-mates straight: an accolade is a single, nameable honor, and plaudits are the individual bursts of praise themselves; acclaim is the weather they add up to.
